Example: Interferon-Beta Stimulated PBMCs

Source: vignettes/ifnb-example.Rmd
ifnb-example.Rmd

This vignette runs the full scoranet workflow on a real dataset and shows every kind of output it produces: console summaries, result tables, files written to disk, network plots, and diagnostic figures.

The data are the interferon-beta stimulated PBMCs from Kang et al. (2018), Nature Biotechnology 36, 89-94, distributed as ifnb by the SeuratData package. Interferon-beta triggers a strong, well-characterised antiviral response, which makes it a good test: the workflow should recover interferon signalling in every cell type.

Setup 

library(scoranet)
library(Seurat)
library(SeuratData)
library(org.Hs.eg.db)
data("ifnb")
ifnb <- UpdateSeuratObject(ifnb)
ifnb <- NormalizeData(ifnb, verbose = FALSE)

table(ifnb$seurat_annotations, ifnb$stim)[c("CD14 Mono", "CD4 Naive T", "B"), ]
#>              
#>               CTRL STIM
#>   CD14 Mono   2215 2147
#>   CD4 Naive T  978 1526
#>   B            407  571

We compare stimulated (STIM) against control (CTRL) cells in three cell types. All output files go to a temporary folder. Every function that writes files takes a directory path with or without a trailing /, and creates the directory if it does not exist.

cell_types <- c("CD14 Mono", "CD4 Naive T", "B")
out_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "ifnb_results")

1. Differential expression

run_cluster_de() runs Seurat::FindMarkers() within each cell type and prints a short summary per cluster.

de_results <- run_cluster_de(
  obj         = ifnb,
  clusters    = cell_types,
  cluster_col = "seurat_annotations",
  ident_col   = "stim",
  ident1      = "STIM",
  ident2      = "CTRL"
)
#> i Running DE for "CD14 Mono" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "CD14 Mono" (STIM vs CTRL) [5.8s]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 1408
#> * DEGs: 704
#> * Up in STIM: 330
#> * Up in CTRL: 374
#> 
#> i Running DE for "CD4 Naive T" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "CD4 Naive T" (STIM vs CTRL) [870ms]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 526
#> * DEGs: 202
#> * Up in STIM: 160
#> * Up in CTRL: 42
#> 
#> i Running DE for "B" (STIM vs CTRL)
#> v Running DE for "B" (STIM vs CTRL) [624ms]
#> 
#> * Tested genes: 812
#> * DEGs: 263
#> * Up in STIM: 187
#> * Up in CTRL: 76
#>

Each cell type returns two tables: degs (genes passing the adjusted p-value and fold-change cutoffs) and tested (every gene FindMarkers tested).

names(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]])
#> [1] "degs"   "tested"

c(degs = nrow(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$degs),
  tested = nrow(de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$tested))
#>   degs tested 
#>    704   1408
top_degs <- de_results[["CD14 Mono"]]$degs
top_degs <- top_degs[order(-abs(top_degs$avg_log2FC)), ]
knitr::kable(
  head(top_degs[, c("gene", "avg_log2FC", "pct.1", "pct.2", "p_val_adj", "res")], 10),
  digits = 3, row.names = FALSE
)
gene avg_log2FC pct.1 pct.2 p_val_adj res
CCL8 7.068 0.918 0.017 0 Upregulated in STIM
CXCL10 7.014 0.984 0.035 0 Upregulated in STIM
ISG15 6.342 1.000 0.324 0 Upregulated in STIM
APOBEC3B 5.151 0.312 0.039 0 Upregulated in STIM
CXCL11 5.087 0.932 0.012 0 Upregulated in STIM
TNFSF10 4.989 0.989 0.047 0 Upregulated in STIM
IFIT3 4.976 0.992 0.056 0 Upregulated in STIM
IFIT1 4.965 0.985 0.033 0 Upregulated in STIM
RSAD2 4.949 0.988 0.045 0 Upregulated in STIM
IFIT2 4.765 0.961 0.039 0 Upregulated in STIM

The strongest changes are classic interferon-stimulated genes and chemokines (CCL8, CXCL10, ISG15, and the IFIT family), exactly what interferon-beta should induce. CD14 monocytes respond most strongly: about half of their tested genes are DEGs.

write_de() saves both tables per cell type:

write_de(de_results, outSubDir = file.path(out_dir, "DE"))
list.files(file.path(out_dir, "DE"))
#> [1] "B_DE_Results.csv"             "B_tested_genes.csv"          
#> [3] "CD14_Mono_DE_Results.csv"     "CD14_Mono_tested_genes.csv"  
#> [5] "CD4_Naive_T_DE_Results.csv"   "CD4_Naive_T_tested_genes.csv"

2. GO over-representation analysis

run_go_ora() runs clusterProfiler::enrichGO() on each cell type’s DEGs. Here each cell type’s tested genes are used as its background (use_tested_universe = TRUE), because genes that were never tested could not have been DEGs.

go_results <- run_go_ora(
  de_list             = de_results,
  org_db              = org.Hs.eg.db,
  use_tested_universe = TRUE,
  ont                 = "BP",
  outputDir           = file.path(out_dir, "ORA")
)
#> 
#> 
#> -- GO set: CD14 Mono --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 2846
#> After filtering: 44
#> Retention proportion: 0.015
#> 
#> -- GO set: CD4 Naive T --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 1520
#> After filtering: 65
#> Retention proportion: 0.043
#> 
#> -- GO set: B --
#> 
#> Genesets tested: 1940
#> After filtering: 90
#> Retention proportion: 0.046

Each element is a standard clusterProfiler enrichResult:

go_cd14 <- as.data.frame(go_results[["CD14 Mono"]])
knitr::kable(
  head(go_cd14[, c("Description", "GeneRatio", "BgRatio", "p.adjust", "Count")], 10),
  digits = 8, row.names = FALSE
)
Description GeneRatio BgRatio p.adjust Count
response to virus 83/640 103/1279 0.00000007 83
defense response to virus 68/640 81/1279 0.00000008 68
biological process involved in interspecies interaction between organisms 183/640 286/1279 0.00005110 183
defense response 182/640 286/1279 0.00008025 182

The top terms are antiviral and cytokine responses.

A QC summary of how many gene sets were tested and retained is attached to the result as its "qc" attribute, and saved as GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv when outputDir is given. outputDir is optional: leave it as NULL to keep everything in R.

knitr::kable(attr(go_results, "qc"), row.names = FALSE)
set tested retained prop
CD14 Mono 2846 44 0.015
CD4 Naive T 1520 65 0.043
B 1940 90 0.046

CD14 monocytes have the most DEGs but the fewest enriched terms. With the tested-gene background, half of their background genes are DEGs, so a term needs a very large share of DEGs to stand out. This is the tested-gene universe being appropriately conservative, not a lack of signal.

write_go() saves the results, adding numeric gene-ratio columns:

write_go(go_results, outSubDir = file.path(out_dir, "ORA"))
list.files(file.path(out_dir, "ORA"))
#> [1] "B_GO_ORA_Results.csv"           "CD14_Mono_GO_ORA_Results.csv"  
#> [3] "CD4_Naive_T_GO_ORA_Results.csv" "GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv"

3. Choosing network settings

Before building the final networks, the diagnostics show how the overlap threshold and Leiden resolution shape them. A first pass at the default settings is enough to run them (the console summary is hidden here).

net_default <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list     = go_results,
  de_list     = de_results,
  comp_label  = "STIM_vs_CTRL",
  base_outdir = file.path(out_dir, "default")
)

dx_default <- run_network_diagnostics(net_default, de_results, go_results)

Overlap threshold

Two GO terms are connected when the Jaccard overlap of their DE genes is at least overlap_threshold; terms with no connection are dropped.

dx_default$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$overlap_threshold

plot of chunk diag-threshold

Almost every pair of enriched terms shares at least one gene, and many share only a few. Raising the threshold from the default 0.1 to 0.2 roughly halves the number of edges while dropping only two terms, so we use 0.2. See DIAGNOSTICS.md in the package repository for a full guide to reading these figures.

4. Pathway overlap networks

We rebuild the networks with the chosen threshold.

net_results <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list           = go_results,
  de_list           = de_results,
  comp_label        = "STIM_vs_CTRL",
  base_outdir       = out_dir,
  overlap_threshold = 0.2,
  leiden_resolution = 1,
  theme_min_terms   = 2
)
names(net_results)
#> [1] "CD14 Mono"   "CD4 Naive T" "B"

Leiden resolution

With the threshold settled, the resolution sweep checks the clustering:

dx <- run_network_diagnostics(net_results, de_results, go_results)
dx$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$leiden_sweep

plot of chunk diag-sweep

A good resolution sits on a plateau where the cluster count is steady, modularity is high, and stability (agreement between random seeds, measured as the adjusted Rand index) is close to 1. Section 7 defines each metric. Here the default resolution of 1 sits at the modularity peak with perfect stability, so we keep it. Modularity is modest because nearly every term in this network is part of one connected interferon response.

If the sweep pointed to a different resolution, recluster_network() would re-run Leiden on the existing network without rebuilding it, keeping the node layout so plots before and after are directly comparable:

net_fine <- recluster_network(net_results[["CD14 Mono"]], resolution = 1.5)
net_fine$cluster_stats
#>   cluster avg_degree n_terms
#> 1       1   30.50000       2
#> 2       2   20.85714       7
#> 3       3   20.50000       4
#> 4       4   25.66667       3
#> 5       5    1.00000       2
#> 6       6   13.35714      14
#> 7       7   10.33333       3
#> 8       8   16.28571       7

Each network result holds the igraph object, tables of terms and clusters, the settings used, and the node layout. plot_network() draws it as one of four editable ggplot objects: regulation, leiden, zscore or themes.

net <- net_results[["CD14 Mono"]]
net
#> <scoranet_network> STIM_vs_CTRL_CD14_Mono
#>   Nodes: 42  Edges: 350  Clusters: 4
#>   Leiden resolution: 1 (modularity)  Overlap threshold: 0.2
#>   Plot with plot_network(); tables with network_tables().
names(net)
#>  [1] "network"            "clustering"         "overlap_matrix"     "go_term_df"        
#>  [5] "cluster_stats"      "leiden_resolution"  "objective_function" "overlap_threshold" 
#>  [9] "seed"               "term_genes"         "cluster_themes"     "cluster_palette"   
#> [13] "layout"             "collection_name"    "ident1"             "ident2"            
#> [17] "file_stem"          "theme_args"

Direction

Nodes are GO terms, coloured by whether their DE genes go up in STIM (red), up in CTRL (blue), or both (grey, “mixed”). Edge width shows overlap; node size shows the number of DE genes in the term. Almost the whole network is red: stimulation switches on the antiviral program.

plot_network(net, "regulation")

plot of chunk plot-regulation

The zscore plot shows how strongly each term leans one way, on a continuous scale. The darkest red terms are the core defence and innate immune terms of the interferon response. The four blue terms, up in CTRL, form the two small clusters (translation and the broad proliferation terms); one pale term in the immune cluster is mixed, with about as many genes going up as down.

plot_network(net, "zscore")

plot of chunk plot-zscore

Leiden clusters 

plot_network(net, "leiden")

plot of chunk plot-leiden

Cluster themes

The themes plot outlines each Leiden cluster and labels it with the GO terms its members fall under in the GO hierarchy, with how many of the cluster’s terms they cover. The two large clusters separate the direct antiviral response (viral process, response to type I interferon) from the broader innate immune response. Of the two small clusters, translation is clearly down in STIM. The other holds two broad “regulation of cell population proliferation” terms; it leans only weakly down and is built from cytokine, chemokine and matrix genes that carry proliferation annotations (see the driver genes below), so it is better read as an annotation catch-all than as a change in proliferation.

plot_network(net, "themes", min_terms = 2)

plot of chunk plot-themes

The labels are also available as a table, along with alternative label styles (keywords, phrase, hub, chosen in the plot with label_by):

knitr::kable(net$cluster_themes[, c("cluster", "n_terms", "ancestor",
                                    "ancestor_n_covered", "hub")])
cluster n_terms ancestor ancestor_n_covered hub
1 16 viral process / response to type I interferon 12 defense response to virus
2 22 response to biotic stimulus / response to peptide 13 innate immune response
3 2 translation 2 cytoplasmic translation
4 2 regulation of cell population proliferation 2 regulation of cell population proliferation

Term-level results

go_term_df lists every term in the network with its cluster and direction statistics. It is also saved, with each term’s DE genes, as <cell type>-cluster-membership.csv, and the cluster labels as <cell type>-cluster-themes.csv. network_tables(net) returns every saved table in R:

knitr::kable(
  head(net$go_term_df[order(-net$go_term_df$degree),
                      c("go_term", "cluster", "degree", "regulation",
                        "n_up", "n_down", "zscore", "median_log2FC")], 8),
  digits = 2, row.names = FALSE
)
go_term cluster degree regulation n_up n_down zscore median_log2FC
defense response to virus 1 31 up 63 5 7.03 1.24
response to virus 1 30 up 69 14 6.04 1.19
innate immune response 2 28 up 94 22 6.69 1.00
defense response to symbiont 2 25 up 106 28 6.74 1.00
biological process involved in interspecies interaction between organisms 2 24 up 129 54 5.54 0.84
defense response to other organism 2 24 up 109 31 6.59 1.00
immune response 2 24 up 129 44 6.46 0.86
regulation of response to external stimulus 2 24 up 81 35 4.27 0.80

5. Interpreting modules

Driver genes

Which genes is each cluster built on? A gene’s share is the fraction of the cluster’s terms that contain it (defined in Section 7).

dx$networks[["CD14 Mono"]]$driver_genes

plot of chunk diag-drivers

The antiviral cluster is built on the OAS and IFITM families. The innate immune cluster shares OAS1 and OAS3 and adds GBP5 and CASP1, all up in STIM. IL1B also runs through most of its terms but goes down (log2FC about -2.7): type I interferon is known to suppress IL-1β production (Guarda et al. 2011, Immunity), so this module is an interferon-driven innate response, not an IL-1β-driven one. The translation cluster is built on ribosomal protein genes that go down after stimulation, and the small “proliferation” cluster on CXCL10, TNFSF13B and CD38 (up) with IL1B and VCAN (down).

Overview across cell types 

dx$overview

plot of chunk diag-overview

CD14 monocytes have by far the most DEGs, split almost evenly between directions, while the T and B cells respond mostly upward.

Word clouds

write_cluster_wordclouds_patchwork() saves a word cloud of term names for each cluster:

write_cluster_wordclouds_patchwork(
  net_list   = net_results["CD14 Mono"],
  outputDir  = out_dir,
  comparison = "STIM_vs_CTRL"
)

plot of chunk wordclouds-include

Terms in one module

write_cluster_results() returns every term in the same cluster as a term of interest. Here, the module containing the most connected term:

top_term <- net$go_term_df$go_term[which.max(net$go_term_df$degree)]
top_term
#> [1] "defense response to virus"

module <- write_cluster_results(net, go_term = top_term, outdir = NULL)
knitr::kable(head(module[, c("go_term", "cluster", "degree", "regulation")], 10),
             row.names = FALSE)
go_term cluster degree regulation
response to virus 1 30 up
defense response to virus 1 31 up
viral life cycle 1 20 up
viral process 1 20 up
regulation of viral process 1 19 up
regulation of viral life cycle 1 18 up
viral genome replication 1 14 up
regulation of viral genome replication 1 14 up
antiviral innate immune response 1 7 up
response to type I interferon 1 13 up

6. Splitting by direction

With split_direction = TRUE, ORA runs separately on up- and down-regulated genes, and a network is built for each direction. Each test is then made against fewer, more coherent genes, which helps in two cases: when one direction has far fewer DEGs and would be drowned out by the other, and, as here, when DEGs make up a large share of the background (half of the tested genes in CD14 monocytes, see Section 2), which dilutes a combined test. Every module in a split network also has a single direction.

go_split <- run_go_ora(
  de_list             = de_results["CD14 Mono"],
  org_db              = org.Hs.eg.db,
  use_tested_universe = TRUE,
  split_direction     = TRUE,
  outputDir           = file.path(out_dir, "ORA_split")
)

net_split <- run_comparison_networks(
  go_list           = go_split,
  de_list           = de_results,
  comp_label        = "STIM_vs_CTRL_split",
  base_outdir       = out_dir,
  overlap_threshold = 0.2,
  split_direction   = TRUE
)
names(net_split)
#> [1] "CD14 Mono_up"   "CD14 Mono_down"
plot_network(net_split[["CD14 Mono_up"]], "themes")

plot of chunk split-up

Built from the up-regulated genes alone, the CD14 monocyte response resolves into many distinct modules: type I interferon production, interleukin-1 production, chemokine response and leukocyte chemotaxis, adaptive immune activation, and more. Most of these terms were not enriched in the combined analysis at all: it found 44 enriched terms, while the up-regulated genes alone give 178. The interleukin-1 production module reflects regulators of IL-1 that go up (such as GBP5 and CASP1), not IL1B itself, which goes down.

The down-regulated genes give a much smaller network of 5 terms (translation and ribosome biogenesis), the same signal as the translation cluster in the combined network.

7. Reading the results

This section defines every quantity the workflow reports and every column in the files it writes.

How the network is built

Jaccard overlap. Each GO term is represented by its DE genes: the genes annotated to the term that are also in the DEG list. For two terms with DE gene sets AA and BB, the Jaccard overlap is

J(A,B)=|A∩B||A∪B|,J(A, B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|A \cup B|},

the number of DE genes the terms share divided by the number of DE genes in either. It runs from 0 (no shared genes) to 1 (identical gene sets). For example, a term with DE genes {ISG15, IFIT1, IFIT3, MX1} and one with {IFIT1, IFIT3, OAS1} share 2 of 5 distinct genes, so J=0.4J = 0.4.

Edges. Two terms are connected when J≥J \geoverlap_threshold (0.2 here), and the edge width shows JJ. Terms with no edge at that threshold are isolates and are dropped from the network.

Node size grows with the number of DE genes in the term (on a log scale).

Degree is the number of other terms a term is connected to. High-degree terms are hubs: their genes overlap with many other terms, which is typical of broad parent terms such as “immune response”.

Direction

For each term, using only its DE genes:

  • n_up and n_down are the numbers of genes with positive and negative log2 fold change (up in STIM and up in CTRL here).
  • avg_log2FC and median_log2FC are the mean and median log2 fold change. The median is less affected by one gene with an extreme fold change.
  • The direction z-score is z=nup−ndownnup+ndown.z = \frac{n_{up} - n_{down}}{\sqrt{n_{up} + n_{down}}}. It combines how consistently the genes move with how many genes support it: 9 up and 1 down gives z=2.5z = 2.5; 3 up and 2 down gives z=0.45z = 0.45; a single up gene gives z=1z = 1.
  • regulation calls a term up when z≥z \gezscore_threshold (default 1), down when z≤−z \le -zscore_threshold, and mixed otherwise.

This direction z-score is not the same as the zScore column that clusterProfiler adds to the ORA results, which measures enrichment, not direction (see below).

Clustering

Leiden clustering groups terms that are more densely connected to each other than to the rest of the network. Edge weights (JJ) are used, so strongly overlapping terms pull harder.

Resolution sets how finely the network is split: higher values give more, smaller clusters.

Modularity scores how well a partition separates the network. It is the share of edge weight that falls within clusters, minus the share expected if edges were placed at random while keeping each term’s total edge weight. Values near 0 mean no better than random; values above about 0.3 indicate clear structure. The sweep always reports standard modularity (resolution 1), so it can be compared across resolutions.

Adjusted Rand index (ARI) measures how well two partitions of the same terms agree. It counts pairs of terms that both partitions put together, or both keep apart, and corrects for the agreement expected by chance. It is 1 when the partitions are identical and about 0 when they agree no more than random partitions would. Stability in the sweep is the mean ARI over every pair of random seeds at a resolution. A value of 1 means the clustering does not depend on the seed.

Cluster themes and the ratios on the network

Each cluster is labelled with up to two GO terms that its terms fall under in the GO hierarchy (its “ancestors”). A label such as

viral process / response to type I interferon (12/16)

means that 12 of the cluster’s 16 terms are one of these ancestors or a descendant of one. An ancestor is only used if it covers at least theme_ancestor_min_share of the cluster (default 15%) and has at most theme_ancestor_max_size descendant terms (default 1,000, to exclude very generic terms). Among those, ancestors are picked one at a time to cover as many still-uncovered terms as possible, weighted by how specific they are. When no ancestor qualifies, the label falls back to the hub term and says “(hub; no shared GO parent)”, which often means the cluster mixes unrelated terms.

The other label styles (label_by in plot_network()) are:

  • keywords: the most distinctive words in the cluster’s term names, down-weighting words common to all clusters.
  • phrase: the top term name, after merging near-identical names.
  • hub: the cluster’s highest-degree term.

Driver genes

For each cluster cc with NcN_c terms, a gene’s share is

share(g,c)=nterms(g,c)Nc,\text{share}(g, c) = \frac{n_{terms}(g, c)}{N_c},

where nterms(g,c)n_{terms}(g, c) is the number of the cluster’s terms whose DE genes include gg. The genes with the highest ntermsn_{terms} are the cluster’s drivers (ties are broken by larger |log⁡2FC||\log_2 FC|). Dot colour is the gene’s log2 fold change, and dot size spans the range of shares shown, so read exact values from the legend.

A high share means a gene is annotated to most of the cluster’s terms, so the cluster’s theme rests on it. It does not mean the gene is specific to that cluster: broadly annotated genes such as IL1B can drive several clusters, and in a two-term cluster every shared gene has a share of 100%.

Output files

Differential expression (DE/)

<cell type>_DE_Results.csv holds the DEGs and <cell type>_tested_genes.csv every gene FindMarkers() tested. Columns:

Column Meaning
p_val Unadjusted p-value (Wilcoxon rank-sum test by default)
avg_log2FC log2 fold change of mean expression, ident1 vs ident2; positive = higher in ident1
pct.1, pct.2 Fraction of cells expressing the gene in ident1 and ident2
p_val_adj Bonferroni-adjusted p-value (over all genes in the dataset)
gene, cluster, comparison Gene symbol, cell type, and "<ident1>_vs_<ident2>"
res DEGs only: "Upregulated in <ident1>" or "Upregulated in <ident2>"

A gene is a DEG when p_val_adj ≤\lepadj_thresh (0.05) and ||avg_log2FC|>| >logfc_thresh (0.5).

GO over-representation (ORA/)

<cell type>_GO_ORA_Results.csv holds one row per enriched GO term:

Column Meaning
ID, Description GO ID and term name
GeneRatio k/nk/n: DEGs in the term / DEGs annotated to any tested GO term
BgRatio M/NM/N: background genes in the term / background genes annotated to any tested GO term
RichFactor k/Mk/M: the fraction of the term’s background genes that are DEGs
FoldEnrichment (k/n)/(M/N)(k/n) / (M/N): how many times more often the term appears among DEGs than in the background
zScore Enrichment z-score from clusterProfiler: how far kk is above the count expected by chance, in standard deviations. Not the direction z-score
pvalue One-sided hypergeometric test p-value
p.adjust Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-value; terms with p.adjust < 0.05 enter the network
qvalue Storey q-value
geneID The term’s DEGs, separated by /
Count kk, the number of DEGs in the term
geneRatio_num, geneRatio_den kk and nn as numbers, added by write_go()

The background is every gene tested in the cell type when use_tested_universe = TRUE. Only GO terms with 5 to 300 annotated background genes are tested. GO_ORA_QC_summary.csv (written when run_go_ora() is given an outputDir, and always available in R as attr(go_results, "qc")) lists, for each cell type, how many GO terms were tested, how many were retained as significant, and the proportion (prop); with simplify = TRUE it adds after_simplify, the count left after redundant terms are merged.

Networks (<comparison>/networks/)

File One row per Columns
<cell type>_network_summary.csv metric nodes, edges and clusters counts
<cell type>-cluster-stats.csv cluster cluster; avg_degree, the mean degree of its terms (how densely connected it is); n_terms
<cell type>-cluster-membership.csv GO term go_term, cluster, degree, regulation, avg_log2FC, median_log2FC, n_up, n_down, zscore (direction), go_id, leiden_resolution, and genes (the term’s DE genes, separated by /). Sorted by cluster, then degree
<cell type>-cluster-themes.csv cluster cluster, n_terms, ancestor (names joined by /), ancestor_id, ancestor_n_covered (the numerator in the plot labels), keywords, phrase, hub

network_tables(net) returns the same four tables in R. The PNG files are the four plot_network() types: -regulation, -clustered-leiden, -zscore and -themes.

8. Files written

Everything the workflow saved to disk:

files <- list.files(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
files[!grepl("^default/", files)]
